{{Short description|Scottish-Australian mathematician}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2019}}

[[File:Horatio Scott Carslaw.gif|thumb|Horatio Scott Carslaw]]
Dr '''Horatio Scott Carslaw''' [[FRSE]] LLD (12 February 1870, [[Helensburgh]], [[Dunbartonshire]], [[Scotland]] &ndash; 11 November 1954, [[Burradoo]], [[New South Wales]], [[Australia]]) was a [[Scotland|Scottish]]-[[Australia]]n mathematician.<ref name=ADB>{{cite AuDB | first = J. C. | last = Jaeger | authorlink = John Conrad Jaeger | title = Carslaw, Horatio Scott (1870–1954) | volume = 7 | year = 1979 | id2 = carslaw-horatio-scott-5518}}</ref><ref>{{acad|id=CRSW891HS|name=Carslaw, Horatio Scott}}</ref>  The book he wrote with his colleague [[John Conrad Jaeger]], ''Conduction of Heat in Solids'', remains a classic in the field.

==Early life and education==
Carslaw was born in [[Helensburgh]], Scotland, the son of the Rev Dr William Henderson Carslaw<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Carslaw.html|title=Horatio Carslaw - Biography}}</ref> (a Free Church minister) and his wife, Elizabeth Lockhead.<ref name="ADB"/> He was educated at [[The Glasgow Academy]]. He went on to study at [[Cambridge University]] and then obtained a postgraduate doctorate at [[Glasgow University]].

== Career ==
Carslaw was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1901.<ref name="royalsoced.org.uk">{{Cite book |url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf |title=Former Fellows of The Royal Society of Edinburgh, 1783–2002: Part 1 (A–J) |author=C D Waterston |author2=A Macmillan Shearer |publisher=[[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] |isbn=090219884X |date=July 2006 |access-date=18 September 2015 |archive-date=24 January 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref> He was a Fellow of [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]] and worked as a lecturer in Mathematics at Glasgow University when, in late 1902, he moved to Australia.<ref>{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=University intelligence |date=7 November 1902 |page=3 |issue=36919}}</ref>

In 1903, upon the retirement of Theodore Thomas Gurney,<ref>{{acad|id=GNY869|name=Gurney, Theodore Thomas}}</ref> Carslaw was appointed Professor and the Chair of Pure and Applied Mathematics in the now [[Sydney School of Mathematics and Statistics|School of Mathematics and Statistics]] at the [[University of Sydney]]. He retired in 1935<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/About/|title = About the School}}</ref> to his house in Burradoo where he produced most of his best work.<ref name="ADB" /> The Carslaw Building at the University, completed in the 1960s and containing the school, is named after him.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths.usyd.edu.au/u/About/Carslaw.html|title = Our home}}</ref>

== Personal life and death ==
Carslaw married Ethel Maude Clarke (daughter of [[Sir William Clarke, 1st Baronet]]<ref name="ADB" />) in 1907 but she died later in the same year.<ref name="royalsoced.org.uk" />

Carslaw died at home in [[Burradoo, New South Wales]] and was buried in the Anglican section of [[Bowral Cemetery]] in [[Bowral]], New South Wales.<ref name="ADB" />
